name: Publius Acilius Attianus
summary:
Publius Acilius Attianus, also known as Caelius Attianus, was a prominent Roman official who played a pivotal role in the transfer of power from Trajan to Hadrian. Born during the reign of Augustus (27 BCE - 14 CE), Attianus rose through the ranks of the imperial administration, eventually becoming an influential advisor to both Trajan and Hadrian.

Attianus' significance lies in his ability to navigate the complex web of alliances and rivalries within the Roman aristocracy. His actions contributed to the eventual succession of Hadrian as emperor, shaping the trajectory of Roman history for decades to come. The specifics of Attianus' role remain somewhat obscure due to the limited surviving records from this period.

Attianus' legacy is also reflected in his writings, particularly his treatise on Stoic philosophy. His philosophical works offer valuable insights into the intellectual currents of late antiquity, shedding light on the cultural and theological debates of the time.

causes: A tumultuous succession crisis following Trajan's death in 117 CE led to a power vacuum that Attianus expertly navigated.
The complexities of Roman imperial politics during this period were further complicated by the intrigues of various factions vying for influence within the imperial court.

The economic strain of maintaining the extensive Roman Empire, coupled with external threats from Parthia and Germania, created an environment in which charismatic leaders like Attianus could emerge to shape the future.
effects: The appointment of Hadrian as emperor marked a significant shift in Roman policy, leading to increased emphasis on military conquests and imperial expansion.
The influence of Stoic philosophy under Hadrian's patronage led to a resurgence of interest in this school of thought among the Roman aristocracy.
Attianus' writings on Stoicism also contributed to the development of philosophical debates during the late antique period, influencing thinkers like Plotinus and Epictetus.
